units.title: Unit 57 — Politics
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 57. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe voting, secret ballots, general elections, constituencies and representation in the UK context.
Distinguish politics, politician, political, power and powerful and related word families.
Explain political parties, government, leaders, policies and the phrase in power.
Use provide, reduce, support, care, tax, fair and equal in discussing policy proposals.
Apply patterns such as vote for someone, provide someone with something and treat people equally.

items.example: She became interested in politics at university.
items.note: The activity and ideas involved in governing a country; usually treated as a singular subject.

items.example: The politician answered questions about education.
items.note: A person active in politics, often holding or seeking public office.

items.example: Education is an important political issue.
items.note: An adjective used before nouns such as party, issue, system and beliefs.

items.example: Millions of people vote in a general election.
items.note: A verb or noun for expressing a choice in an election.

items.example: Many residents voted for the same candidate.
items.note: Use vote for a candidate or party, not vote a candidate.

items.example: Several MPs voted against the proposed law.
items.note: Contrast vote against a proposal with vote for a candidate.

items.example: The members chose their leader by secret ballot.
items.note: The voter’s choice is private; ballot can mean the voting process or ballot paper.

items.word: put a cross on the ballot paper
items.pt: marcar um X na cédula de votação
items.ipa: /pʊt ə krɒs ɒn ðə ˈbælət ˈpeɪpə/
items.example: Please put a cross on the ballot paper beside your choice.
items.note: An X can indicate a selected option on a paper ballot.

items.example: An election will be held later this year.
items.note: An organised process in which people choose representatives by voting.

items.example: Several parties took part in the general election.
items.note: In the book's UK context, a national election for members of Parliament.

items.example: Voters elect representatives for their area.
items.note: Verb meaning choose someone through a vote; related noun election.

items.example: The organisation will hold an election in November.
items.note: Use hold with election; past and passive forms are held and be held.

items.example: The election will be held on a Thursday.
items.note: Passive form commonly used for formal events and elections.

items.example: Each constituency chooses a representative.
items.note: An area whose voters elect a member of a parliament or assembly.

items.example: She joined a political party while studying.
items.note: An organisation with shared political ideas that seeks public office.

items.example: Parliament discussed the proposal for several hours.
items.note: A national legislature; the book uses the UK Parliament as its example.

items.example: Our Member of Parliament visited a local school.
items.note: A person elected to sit in Parliament; abbreviated to MP.

items.example: The local MP answered residents' questions.
items.note: British abbreviation for Member of Parliament; say the letters M and P.

items.example: Residents contacted their elected representative.
items.note: A person chosen to act or speak on behalf of others.

items.example: The government announced a new education policy.
items.note: People and institutions responsible for governing a country.

items.example: The winning party was invited to form a government.
items.note: Establish a governing administration after an election.

items.example: The party leader spoke at the conference.
items.note: A person in charge of a group, party or organisation.

items.example: The party has been in power for several years.
items.note: In control of government; compare power as a noun.

items.example: The Prime Minister met several regional leaders.
items.note: The head of government in the UK and various other parliamentary systems.

items.example: The new government took power after the election.
items.note: Noun for control or authority; related adjective powerful.

items.example: The president is a powerful political figure.
items.note: Adjective related to power; describes having influence or control.

items.pt: acreditar em algo; defender uma ideia
items.example: I believe in equal opportunities for everyone.
items.note: Believe in an idea means think it is right, valuable or desirable.

items.example: Her belief in public education is strong.
items.note: Noun from believe; plural beliefs, not believes.

items.example: People with different political beliefs can still cooperate.
items.note: A person's views about society and government.

items.pt: política pública; diretriz; proposta de ação
items.example: The party announced a policy on housing.
items.note: A plan or set of principles for decisions and action; plural policies.

items.example: The parties presented different policies on transport.
items.note: Plural of policy; not the same as politics or police.

items.example: The council provides free training courses.
items.note: Give or make a service or resource available.

items.example: The charity provides families with warm clothing.
items.note: Pattern: provide someone with something.

items.example: The school provides meals for its pupils.
items.note: Alternative pattern: provide something for someone.

items.example: The council plans to improve nursery education.
items.note: Education for young children before primary school; British English.

items.example: Older people may need additional care at home.
items.note: Looking after someone; often uncountable in this sense.

items.example: The centre provides care for elderly people.
items.note: The source exercises practise provide care for old people.

items.example: Local volunteers support families in difficulty.
items.note: Noun or verb; support can mean practical, social or financial help.

items.example: The service offers transport for elderly residents.
items.note: Polite adjective for older people; the elderly is a collective noun.

items.example: The government aims to reduce unemployment.
items.note: The situation of being without paid work; generally uncountable.

items.example: The city plans to reduce waiting times.
items.note: Make an amount or level smaller; similar in meaning to cut.

items.example: There was a reduction in the tax rate.
items.note: Noun from reduce; commonly a reduction in something.

items.example: The council decided to cut unnecessary costs.
items.note: Verb meaning reduce; cut-cut-cut.

items.example: Most residents want a fair tax system.
items.note: Treating people reasonably and without unjust discrimination.

items.example: Many workers considered the new rule unfair.
items.note: Opposite of fair.

items.example: Some taxes help pay for public services.
items.note: Money paid to government; tax can be a count or mass noun depending on use.

items.example: People discussed changes to the tax system.
items.note: The rules and structures for collecting taxes.

items.example: Above all, the policy should protect children.
items.note: Means most importantly; often used to emphasise a main point.

items.pt: tratar; agir com alguém de determinada forma
items.example: Managers should treat all staff with respect.
items.note: Treat someone fairly, equally or badly; note the manner of behaviour.

items.pt: igual; de igual valor ou importância
items.example: Every citizen should have equal rights.
items.note: Adjective describing the same status, value or importance.

items.example: The teacher treated all students equally.
items.note: Adverb from equal; often after treat.

items.example: Public services should treat people fairly.
items.note: A useful policy collocation; fairly is the adverb formed from fair.

items.example: The organisation promises to treat people equally.
items.note: Use the adverb equally to describe how people are treated.

sectionsChecked: A: Elections in the UK; voting, election process, constituencies, MPs, governing party and leader
A: Language-help noun-person-adjective families: politics, politician, political, power, powerful
B: Political policies; leaflet language, social policy terms, fairness and equality
B: Language-help verb-noun pairs: believe/belief and reduce/reduction

units.title: Unit 58 — Climate change
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 58. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Explain global warming, greenhouse gases, fossil fuels and the greenhouse effect.
Describe environmental changes and their effects, including droughts, floods and harm to species.
Build verb–noun pairs such as create/creation, reduce/reduction and destroy/destruction.
Use practical collocations for recycling, energy efficiency, saving resources and taking action.
Pronounce challenging forms such as flood, fuel, drought, suffer and climate.

items.example: The climate in this area is mild for most of the year.
items.note: The usual weather patterns of a place over a long period; note the unstressed second syllable.

items.example: Scientists study how climate change affects rainfall.
items.note: Long-term change in climate patterns, including temperature and rainfall.

items.example: The natural greenhouse effect helps keep the Earth warm.
items.note: Warming caused when gases in the atmosphere retain some outgoing heat.

items.example: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas.
items.note: A gas that contributes to the greenhouse effect; plural greenhouse gases.

items.example: Transport and industry produce greenhouse gases.
items.note: Plural lexical phrase; examples include carbon dioxide and methane.

items.example: Burning coal releases carbon dioxide into the air.
items.note: A greenhouse gas often abbreviated CO2.

items.example: Methane can escape from some natural gas systems.
items.note: A greenhouse gas mentioned in the book's examples.

items.example: Ozone is a gas found in the atmosphere.
items.note: A gas that occurs in different parts of the atmosphere; its effects depend on location.

items.example: Some greenhouse gases exist naturally.
items.note: Be real or present; related noun existence.

items.example: The existence of rare animals depends on their habitat.
items.note: Noun from exist; included in the word-family exercise.

items.example: Some gases occur naturally in the atmosphere.
items.note: In a way that happens without human intervention.

items.example: These conditions can create serious problems.
items.note: Make something exist or happen; compare creation.

items.pt: sustentar a vida humana; permitir a existência de vida humana
items.example: Clean water and a stable climate support human life.
items.note: Support here means make continuing life possible.

items.example: Coal is a fossil fuel.
items.note: Fuel formed from ancient organic material; often plural fossil fuels.

items.example: Using fossil fuels can release greenhouse gases.
items.note: Group including coal, oil and natural gas.

items.example: The bus uses less fuel than the old model.
items.note: Material or energy source used to provide heat or power; note its pronunciation.

items.example: Oil is used to make many fuels and products.
items.note: In this section, oil refers to petroleum as a fossil fuel.

items.example: Many homes use natural gas for heating.
items.note: A fossil fuel largely composed of methane.

items.example: Some power stations still burn coal.
items.note: A solid fossil fuel formed from ancient plant matter.

items.example: The factory used an excessive amount of water.
items.note: More than is reasonable, necessary or desirable.

items.example: The amount of waste fell after the new rules.
items.note: A quantity, especially with uncountable nouns such as water or energy.

items.example: The result was a sharp increase in costs.
items.note: Something that happens because of an earlier event or condition.

items.example: Global warming can affect oceans and ecosystems.
items.note: Long-term rise in Earth's average temperature.

items.example: The city's average temperature has increased over time.
items.note: The mean temperature across a period or area.

items.pt: registrado; desde o início dos registros
items.example: It was one of the warmest days on record.
items.note: Recorded in reliable observations or official information.

items.example: Very heavy rain can occur in spring.
items.note: A formal verb meaning happen; past occurred, with double r.

items.example: One effect of a drought is reduced food production.
items.note: A result or change caused by something; contrast affect (verb).

items.example: A long drought damaged crops in the region.
items.note: A prolonged period with too little rain; gh is silent.

items.example: The flood damaged several houses near the river.
items.note: Water covering normally dry land; rhymes with blood, not food.

items.example: Several roads were closed because of flooding.
items.note: The process or situation of being flooded; related to flood.

items.pt: sofrer; passar por dificuldade ou dano
items.example: Some plants suffer during very dry summers.
items.note: Experience something difficult, painful or harmful.

items.example: The project aims to reduce unnecessary suffering.
items.note: Noun from suffer; included in the book's word-family task.

items.example: Several species of bird live near the lake.
items.note: The form species is used for both singular and plural.

items.example: Some species may disappear if their habitats are lost.
items.note: Stop existing or stop being seen; intransitive verb.

items.example: A severe storm can destroy buildings.
items.note: Damage so badly that something cannot be used or no longer exists.

items.example: The destruction of forests harms wildlife.
items.note: Noun formed from destroy; part of the exercise word family.

items.example: Everyone can help protect the environment.
items.note: The natural world around us, including air, land and water.

items.example: Carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere when fuel burns.
items.note: The layer of gases surrounding Earth.

items.example: The team discussed possible solutions to the problem.
items.note: A way of dealing successfully with a problem; noun from solve.

items.example: Communities are working together to solve the problem.
items.note: Verb related to solution; solve a problem, not solution a problem.

items.example: The programme aims to reduce energy use.
items.note: Make an amount, level or number smaller; noun reduction.

items.example: The town reported a reduction in household waste.
items.note: Noun from reduce; exercise pairing reduce–reduction.

items.example: We need to act before the problem becomes worse.
items.note: Do something, rather than only talk about a problem.

items.example: Local communities can take action to save water.
items.note: Fixed expression meaning do something to solve or improve a situation.

items.example: Countries need to act together on shared problems.
items.note: Cooperate by taking action as a group.

items.example: The new system will arrive next month; in the meantime, use the old one.
items.note: During the period before another event happens.

items.example: Every individual can make small changes at home.
items.note: A single person rather than a group; also an adjective.

items.example: Don't throw old bottles away if you can recycle them.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb: throw it away, not throw away it.

items.example: Our school recycles paper and plastic.
items.note: Process used material so that it can be used again.

items.example: Recycling can reduce the amount of waste we produce.
items.note: Noun derived from recycle; appears in the exercise family.

items.example: We save energy by switching off unused lights.
items.note: Use less energy rather than wasting it.

items.example: Heating the building requires energy.
items.note: Power used to operate equipment and provide heating.

items.example: Don't waste clean water when washing dishes.
items.note: Verb and noun with the same spelling; often used with water or energy.

items.example: Leaving the tap running can waste water.
items.note: Here waste is a verb; waste water can also mean used water in a different context.

items.example: Please turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.
items.note: Turn off describes stopping a water or electrical flow.

items.example: The kitchen tap was leaking.
items.note: British English; the American English equivalent is often faucet.

items.example: Switch off the lights before you leave the room.
items.note: Switch off is separable: switch them off.

items.example: We turn off the lights when the office is empty.
items.note: Common alternative to switch off the lights.

items.example: We replaced an old light bulb yesterday.
items.note: The replaceable device that produces light in a lamp.

items.pt: eficiente em termos energéticos; de baixo consumo
items.example: An energy-efficient fridge uses less electricity.
items.note: Describes equipment that does useful work without wasting much energy.

items.example: The new heating system is more efficient.
items.note: Works well while using little wasted time, effort or energy.

items.example: Volunteers plan to plant trees near the school.
items.note: Plant means put young trees or seeds into the ground.

items.word: reduce the amount of carbon dioxide
items.pt: reduzir a quantidade de dióxido de carbono
items.example: The project aims to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide released.
items.note: Pattern from the source's environmental advice: reduce the amount of + uncountable noun.

items.example: Local groups support projects to protect rivers.
items.note: Verb and noun; can mean help people, organisations or living systems.

B: The solution; illustrated six-point environmental actions, recycling, energy and resources
